title: Diagnosing respiratory illness in a chicken flock
subtitle: Sneezing, wheezing, and nasal discharge can be Mycoplasma, infectious bronchitis, or Newcastle disease. The pattern across the flock is the first clue.
excerpt: Respiratory illness in chickens often announces itself as a wave: one or two birds showing nasal discharge and reduced activity, followed by the rest of the flock over 48-3 days. How fast it spreads, whether it affects egg production, and whether mortality follows help distinguish the cause. Here is how to read the outbreak pattern and what to do next.
sourceNotes: DEFRA Codes of Recommendations for the Welfare of Laying Hens, health section. APHA poultry disease recognition guidance. AHDB Poultry respiratory disease fact sheets. Lewis Wright, The Practical Poultry Keeper (1867), Internet Archive, chapter on poultry diseases.

glossaryTerms.definition: Mycoplasma gallisepticum, a chronic bacterial respiratory infection of poultry. Causes nasal discharge, tracheal rattle, and reduced egg production. Spreads slowly within a flock. Not usually fatal but not curable; can be managed with antibiotics.

A viral respiratory disease of chickens (IB virus). Highly contagious: typically spreads through the entire flock within 48 hours. Causes respiratory signs and drops in egg production. Chickens usually recover in 2–3 weeks.
A notifiable viral disease of poultry. Causes respiratory signs, nervous signs, and can produce rapid high mortality. Any suspected Newcastle disease must be reported to APHA immediately.

content.text: Mycoplasma
infectious bronchitis
, and sinusitis from poor ventilation all look similar in a single bird. They differ in how fast they spread, what else they affect, and how to respond.
Newcastle disease
is a notifiable outlier. Knowing the difference matters.
The pattern of spread
Mycoplasma:
Slow spread, weeks. First bird and last bird separated by 1-3 weeks. Low mortality. Chronic rattle and discharge persist for months.
Infectious bronchitis:
Rapid spread through the whole flock within 48-72 hours. Usually all birds affected at once. Egg production drops sharply for 1-3 weeks. Mortality usually low in healthy adults.
Environmental / sinusitis:
Affects some birds, not all. Often linked to damp conditions or sudden weather change. No mortality. Clears with improved ventilation in 1-2 weeks.
Newcastle disease:
Very rapid spread and high mortality. Nervous signs (twisted necks, circling, paralysis) alongside respiratory signs. Call APHA immediately.
What to check on affected birds
Nasal discharge: clear or mucoid? Mycoplasma produces mucoid discharge and a bubbling sound in the trachea. IB produces a more watery discharge with snicking.
Swollen sinuses under the eyes? This is more typical of Mycoplasma and Avian influenza than IB.
Are the birds eating? IB-affected birds usually continue eating. Mycoplasma birds show partial inappetence. A bird that has completely stopped eating is more seriously ill.
Any nervous signs: head tilt, circling, falling over, twisted neck? These indicate Newcastle disease or Marek's disease, both serious. Isolate the affected bird and call a vet.
When to call a vet or report
Suspected
Newcastle disease
must be reported to APHA (03000 200 301). Report if the flock shows rapid spread with deaths, respiratory signs alongside nervous signs, or sudden unexplained deaths with any respiratory illness.

A vet-confirmed Mycoplasma case can be managed with tylosin or oxytetracycline. IB is viral with no specific drug. Supportive care and reduced stress are the main tools. Environmental sinusitis resolves with better ventilation and lower ammonia.
